speaker: Andre
text_en: I wanted to ask history a question. Not what happened. What it felt like to hear what came next.

speaker: Caesar, offscreen
text_en: Does my name survive?

speaker: Andre
text_en: Your name survives. So do the reforms and the victories people study. But they also study how much power one man can hold—and what happens to a republic around him.

speaker: Caesar, offscreen
text_en: Then they remember a tyrant?

speaker: Andre
text_en: They argue about you. A brilliant commander. An ambitious ruler. I came to ask what victory leaves behind.

speaker: Khan, offscreen
text_en: Will my sons keep what I have made?

speaker: Andre
text_en: They will enlarge it. Routes across Eurasia will carry merchants, ideas, and knowledge. But conquest also leaves ruined cities and families who never return.

speaker: Khan, offscreen
text_en: And what will they call me?

speaker: Andre
text_en: A founder. A conqueror. They will argue about what your empire joined—and what it destroyed. None of those words can make the dead speak.

speaker: Galileo, offscreen
text_en: Am I finally believed?

speaker: Andre
text_en: People learn from you. They also turn you into a simple story: one scientist against a whole world. The truth is harder than that.

speaker: Galileo, offscreen
text_en: And what survives of the question?

speaker: Andre
text_en: Your observations. And the warning in your trial. Silencing a person does not settle a question.

speaker: Napoleon, offscreen
text_en: Does France keep my laws?

speaker: Andre
text_en: Your civil code outlives your throne. Other countries borrow from it. But a law can promise equality and still deny it to someone.

speaker: Napoleon, offscreen
text_en: And do they call me great?

speaker: Andre
text_en: Some do. Others ask about the wars and the power you kept for yourself. When they say greatness, they still argue about the price.

speaker: Oppenheimer, offscreen
text_en: Does the test work?

speaker: Andre
text_en: It works. Weeks later, atomic bombs strike Hiroshima and Nagasaki. People will argue about ending the war, about those who died, and about the fear that follows.

speaker: Oppenheimer, offscreen
text_en: Can you tell me whether it was right?

speaker: Andre
text_en: I can tell you what came next. That is not the same as answering the question.

speaker: Andre
text_en: I went looking for answers in the past. I came back with a question for us. What will they have to tell us about the things we are doing now?
